feature_name: Runtime contracts split from engine (dependency-direction gate)
feature_description: Split ResearchRunRequest, ResearchRunResult, and RunConflictError out of runtime/engine.py into a new runtime/contracts.py, and repoint the four modules that only ever needed the contracts (cli.py, runtime/batch.py, product/research.py, backtest/validation.py) so they stop transitively depending on ResearchEngine's SQLite storage (storage.recovery, storage.sqlite).

notes: Also exercised by test_runtime_contracts_module_does_not_import_runtime_engine, test_runtime_contracts_module_does_not_transitively_depend_on_storage, and test_contract_only_consumers_do_not_transitively_reach_engine_owned_storage_modules in tests/unit/test_import_layering.py, all using grimp.build_graph per the existing Task-4 idiom, not runtime sys.modules introspection. Verified by mutation: reverting any one of the four modules' import line back to `from openalpha_cn.runtime.engine import ...` makes the direct-edge test fail. The transitive-storage check is scoped to storage.recovery/storage.sqlite specifically, not all of openalpha_cn.storage, because two of the four modules retain real, pre-existing, unrelated storage touchpoints out of this task's scope: cli.py separately needs backtest.replay.ReplayCorpus (which needs the full ResearchEngine for its `replay` subcommand), and runtime.batch has its own TYPE_CHECKING-only reference to storage.batch.SQLiteBatchTaskStore for an unrelated method parameter. runtime/__init__.py resolves ResearchEngine lazily via a module __getattr__ (PEP 562) instead of an eager top-level import, because Python always executes a package's __init__.py before any of its submodules -- an eager import there would silently reintroduce the storage dependency at real runtime for anyone merely importing runtime.contracts. A reviewer proved that guard previously had no automated backstop: grimp records function-local and eager top-level imports as the same static edge, so it cannot see whether ResearchEngine resolution actually runs at import time. That gap is now closed by tests/unit/runtime/test_contracts_import_isolation.py::test_importing_runtime_contracts_in_a_fresh_process_does_not_load_the_storage_layer, a subprocess-isolated test (launched via sys.executable, so it runs under the same interpreter/venv as the rest of the suite) that imports openalpha_cn.runtime.contracts in a brand-new Python process and asserts openalpha_cn.storage and every submodule under it are absent from that process's real sys.modules -- an in-process check would be meaningless, since pytest has already imported most of openalpha_cn, including the storage layer, by the time any test runs. Verified by mutation: temporarily making runtime/__init__.py's ResearchEngine import eager makes this test fail, naming the leaked openalpha_cn.storage, .memory, .parquet, .recovery, and .sqlite modules; restoring the lazy form makes it pass again. This is a narrow, deliberate exception to the task brief's general prohibition on runtime sys.modules checks: that prohibition targets the dependency-direction assertions above, where grimp's static analysis is the right tool; here static analysis is structurally blind to eager-vs-lazy import timing, so a runtime check is the only tool that can verify this specific property. The test deliberately does not assert bare sqlite3 absence from sys.modules: models/governance.py imports sqlite3 directly at module scope for ModelRegistry's durable usage accounting, reached from runtime.contracts via agents.base -> agents/__init__.py -> agents.model -> models.base -> models/__init__.py -> models.openai_compatible -> models.governance, a separate, already-tracked layering exemption (baseline entry V2-P0B-011, models.governance -> sqlite3) unrelated to ResearchEngine's lazy resolution and out of this task's scope; asserting bare sqlite3 absence would fail permanently regardless of whether the guard under test is eager or lazy, so it would not discriminate the regression this test exists to catch.

feature_name: SQLite schema migration engine (versioned, transactional, backup-and-rollback)
feature_description: Add a forward-only SQLite schema-migration engine for the shared state.sqlite3 that all seven SQLite stores share: PRAGMA user_version is the cheap, atomic current-version marker; a new schema_migrations table (version, name, applied_at) is a human-readable audit trail alongside it. Migrations are a plain, hand-ordered tuple (MIGRATIONS), sorted by version at run time, not a directory-scanning plugin system or alembic -- the runtime dependency set stays at seven packages. run_migrations() applies every pending migration inside its own BEGIN IMMEDIATE/COMMIT transaction (DDL, the audit row, and the PRAGMA user_version bump are one atomic unit); any failure rolls the whole unit back and re-raises MigrationFailedError naming the pre-migration backup, without advancing user_version. run_migrations() always backs up state.sqlite3 (via the SQLite backup API, safe under WAL) to runtime_dir/backups before applying anything pending. A baseline migration (version 1) stamps both a brand-new database and an existing, unversioned v1-shaped database (created before this task existed) at the baseline version without touching data. A demo migration (version 2, demo_add_runs_archived_at) adds a nullable runs.archived_at column, proving the executor can make a real, additive schema change to a table already holding real records while those records stay fully readable through the unmodified SQLiteRunRepository afterwards -- the acceptance proof PRD Story S88 and Testing Decision 16 require. Because migrations run before any store is constructed (the composition-root mount point in runtime/composition.py's build_storage(), per the task brief), a migration that alters a pre-existing table raises MigrationNotYetApplicable against a brand-new install where that table doesn't exist yet; the executor stops without error and retries on the next invocation, once the owning store has created the table. Two new CLI commands, 'openalpha migrate status' and 'openalpha migrate run' (with --dry-run), expose the current version, the applied/pending migration lists, and the backup path.
acceptance_test: tests/integration/storage/test_migrations.py::test_demo_migration_advances_version_and_preserves_v1_records
notes: The core proof is test_demo_migration_advances_version_and_preserves_v1_records: it builds a v1-shaped database using only the pre-existing, unmodified SQLiteRunRepository and SQLiteResearchMemory stores (one run manifest, one decision, one memory entry -- exactly as brief section 5 specifies), confirms it has no version stamp and no schema_migrations table (a real old-shaped library), runs the migration engine, and asserts: user_version advances from 0 to 2, schema_migrations records both migrations by name, runs.archived_at now exists (the real schema change happened), and all three pre-migration records are still readable byte-for-byte through the same unmodified stores. Also exercised by test_running_migrations_again_is_idempotent (a second run applies nothing and takes no new backup), test_demo_migration_is_a_sql_level_no_op_when_the_column_already_exists (covers the migration's own duplicate-column guard, independent of the framework-level already-applied guard), test_new_database_lands_on_baseline_and_defers_the_demo_migration and tests/unit/runtime/test_composition_migrations.py's two tests (proving build_storage() never crashes a brand-new install and catches the deferred migration up on the next call), and tests/integration/test_cli_migrate.py's four tests for 'migrate status', 'migrate run --dry-run', and 'migrate run'. Failure/rollback semantics are proven, not reasoned about, by test_failing_migration_rolls_back_leaves_version_unmoved_and_backup_intact: a deliberately doomed migration (version 3) runs a real ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN and then raises, inside the same BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction as the audit-row insert and the PRAGMA user_version write; the test asserts user_version is unchanged, no schema_migrations row exists for version 3, the doomed column is absent from runs (proving SQLite DDL genuinely rolled back, not just the bookkeeping), the pre-existing run record is still readable, and the pre-migration backup file still exists on disk. A standalone Python experiment (documented in the task report) independently confirmed PRAGMA user_version participates correctly in an explicit BEGIN/ROLLBACK transaction under Python 3.11's sqlite3 module, while PRAGMA journal_mode does not -- it raises OperationalError if executed inside an open transaction at all -- which is why run_migrations() never touches journal_mode itself and leaves WAL-mode setup to each store's own _initialize(), unchanged. No existing CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS statement in any of the seven stores was moved or edited; storage/migrations.py imports only sqlite3 and the standard library, so it adds no new lint-imports edge beyond the pre-existing legal runtime -> storage direction composition.py already uses.

feature_name: Migration engine hardening: CLI convergence, honest status reporting, race-safe execution, collision-free backups, and a fresh-install guard
feature_description: Closes six reviewer-confirmed Important gaps in the V2-P0B-004 migration engine (OA-OPS-021), without changing its deferral design. (1) 'openalpha migrate run' used to call run_migrations() directly, bypassing build_storage() -- it never constructed a store, so a migration deferred only because its owning table did not exist yet (the demo migration on a fresh install) stayed pending forever no matter how many times the command ran. migrate_run now goes through build_storage() -- the same composition root sdk.py/api/app.py use -- so the stores it constructs as a side effect let the next invocation's migration attempt actually converge. (2) migrate_run used to branch on 'not result.applied' alone and print 'up to date' even while read_status().pending was non-empty, contradicting 'migrate status' on the same directory in the same breath; it now checks read_status().pending after running and only ever claims completion when nothing is applied and nothing is pending, otherwise reporting the still-pending migrations by name. (3) Nothing previously forced a future migration to defer safely on a fresh, empty database -- the demo migration was safe only because it hand-wrote a table-exists check. storage/migrations.py now exposes a reusable require_table(connection, name) guard, and a structural test runs every non-baseline migration in the real MIGRATIONS registry against a genuinely empty database, asserting it raises MigrationNotYetApplicable rather than crashing -- so a Phase P4 migration that omits the check fails this test instead of crashing OpenAlphaSDK.__init__/create_app() for every fresh install. (4) '.bak' backup files (SQLite binary dumps, just like '.sqlite3'/'.db'/'.duckdb') were missing from scripts/verify_publication.py's BLOCKED_SUFFIXES, so an untracked '.bak' that escaped .gitignore (e.g. under a custom --runtime-dir) would publish clean; '.bak' is now blocked like its siblings. (5) The pre-migration backup filename ({name}.v{version}.{timestamp}.bak, second precision) had no collision check, so two backups at the same version within the same second silently overwrote each other; _take_backup now claims its filename with os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL (atomic at the OS level, not an exists-then-create race) and falls back to a numeric suffix on collision. (6) run_migrations()'s per-migration loop computed its pending list once, before acquiring any lock, so two concurrent callers on the same runtime_dir (e.g. the API and the CLI) could both decide the same migration was pending; the loser's BEGIN IMMEDIATE would then succeed after the winner committed, replay migration.apply(), and hit a primary-key collision on its own schema_migrations insert -- reported as a genuine MigrationFailedError even though the database had converged correctly. Each loop iteration now re-reads PRAGMA user_version immediately after acquiring the write lock and skips a migration a concurrent winner already committed, instead of replaying it.
acceptance_test: tests/integration/storage/test_migrations.py::test_concurrent_run_migrations_does_not_report_a_false_failure
notes: test_concurrent_run_migrations_does_not_report_a_false_failure races two real, separate OS processes (multiprocessing's spawn start method launches a fresh interpreter, not a thread) against the same fresh database with a deliberately slow migration to force the BEGIN IMMEDIATE contention deterministically (the reviewer's own natural-timing reproduction was 1-in-5); it is confirmed RED against the pre-fix executor (fails 3/3 runs with a false MigrationFailedError) and GREEN against the fix (5/5 runs). test_every_non_baseline_migration_defers_gracefully_on_a_fresh_empty_database is the Finding 1c structural guard: it independently reproduces a bare sqlite3.OperationalError crash when tried against a hand-rolled careless migration missing require_table(), proving the guard has teeth. test_take_backup_does_not_overwrite_an_existing_backup_at_the_same_timestamp is RED against the pre-fix naive filename (both backups collide on the same path) and GREEN against the O_CREAT|O_EXCL fix. test_migrate_run_converges_after_it_constructs_stores_then_reports_up_to_date (tests/integration/test_cli_migrate.py) replaces test_migrate_run_a_second_time_reports_up_to_date, which asserted the Finding 1b lie as correct behaviour; the new test is RED against the pre-fix CLI (first assertion fails: the CLI still claims 'up to date' while genuinely stuck) and GREEN against the fix, and additionally proves Finding 1a's convergence end to end through the real CLI (a second invocation on the same fresh runtime_dir actually applies the demo migration, and only a third, truly-idle invocation reports 'up to date'). test_publication_gate_blocks_sqlite_backup_files pins '.bak' in BLOCKED_SUFFIXES directly; separately verified end to end by placing an untracked reviewer_repro.bak at the repo root and confirming scripts/verify_publication.py now reports it blocked (not committed; a throwaway manual repro).

feature_name: Version-dispatched contract reads: row-content schema upgrade mechanism
feature_description: Version-dispatched reads for stored contract payloads, closing the read-side half of V2-P0B-004/OA-OPS-021's table-migration story: eight contracts carry a literal schema_version field (signal.py:17, run.py:49, decision.py:29, validation.py:28, evidence.py:30, providers/base.py:85,115, storage/recovery.py:24) combined with extra="forbid", so Model.model_validate_json(row) hard-fails the moment a row's schema_version is one this build's Literal does not carry -- in either direction, upgraded code reading an old row or old code reading a row written by a newer build. domain/versioning.py adds ContractVersions[T], a plain per-contract registry (mirroring storage/migrations.py's Migration dataclass, not a versioning framework) mapping every schema_version this build knows to its model plus an upgrade chain to the current version, and read_versioned(), which parses raw JSON with the stdlib json module -- deliberately not pydantic -- to read schema_version out of a plain dict before any model sees the payload, then dispatches, validates at the payload's own version (so a genuinely malformed row still raises its own model's ValidationError, never confused with a version mismatch), and walks the upgrade chain to current_version. An unregistered schema_version raises UnknownSchemaVersionError naming the contract, the payload's version, and every version this build supports -- explicit failure instead of silent misreading, per the brief. All 15 of storage/'s Model.model_validate_json(row[0]) call sites (portfolio.py x2, product.py x3, batch.py x3, sqlite.py x4, memory.py x2, recovery.py x1) now go through read_versioned(); the 7 storage models with no schema_version field (PortfolioTransition, WatchlistEntry, ResearchReport, BatchResearchTask, BatchProgressEvent, CheckpointRecord, MemoryEntry) get a single_version() registry keyed on None -- the value payload.get('schema_version') naturally returns when the key is absent -- so every stored-row read in this package goes through one mechanism, and giving one of these models a real schema_version later is a registry edit at its own definition, not a call-site audit. No v2 of any real contract is created (that is Phase P4's job); the upgrade chain itself is proven end to end with a synthetic, test-only demo-widget v1->v2 contract in tests/unit/domain/test_versioning.py, exactly as storage/migrations.py's demo migration proved the table-migration engine. test_schema_export.py's line-19 assertion, which hardcoded checked_in["properties"]["schema_version"]["const"].endswith("/v1") and would fail by design the moment any contract is upversioned, now compares against each contract's ContractVersions.current_version instead; it still catches an unregenerated schema file via the pre-existing deep checked_in == schema comparison (verified by a manual repro: mutating a checked-in schema's schema_version const away from the runtime model's value reproduces the failure), and additionally now catches a registry whose current_version was never bumped to match a correctly regenerated schema file. A concluded, documented finding for Phase P4: stable_model_id (domain/_identity.py) hashes model_dump(mode='json', exclude_computed_fields=True), and schema_version is a real (non-computed) field, so it participates in the hash for the four contracts whose computed id is built with stable_model_id -- SignalFrame.signal_id, DecisionLedger.decision_id, ValidationResult.validation_id, ProviderRecord.record_id. An upcast that bumps schema_version therefore changes the recomputed id even when every other field is identical, while the row's own stored primary key was computed and written at the old version -- a real migration cutting v2 of any of these four contracts must treat that identity shift as a Task-11-style, auditable, atomic migration (rewriting the stored key), not a transparent read-time illusion. EvidenceSnapshot.evidence_id is the contrasting safe pattern: it is hand-derived from (subject, kind, source_id, timeline.available_time, content_hash) and deliberately excludes schema_version.

Confirmed RED before domain/versioning.py existed: importing it failed with ModuleNotFoundError; confirmed RED again for the storage wiring before the registries existed: ImportError on DECISION_LEDGER_VERSIONS. tests/integration/storage/test_versioned_reads.py proves the hard constraint end to end against real SQLite databases built through today's normal write paths: test_sqlite_run_repository_reads_existing_records_field_for_field and test_sqlite_recovery_store_reads_existing_records_field_for_field append via SQLiteRunRepository/SQLiteRecoveryStore then assert the read_versioned()-routed get_run/get_decision/get_decision_for_run/list_checkpoints/get results equal the originally constructed objects field for field; test_sqlite_run_repository_get_run_fails_loudly_on_an_unknown_schema_version, ..._get_decision_fails_loudly_..., and test_sqlite_recovery_store_get_fails_loudly_on_an_unknown_schema_version hand-insert a row carrying schema_version='<contract>/v2' directly via sqlite3 (bypassing the pydantic model entirely) and assert UnknownSchemaVersionError names the contract, the found version, and the supported set -- reproducing, with a real database, the 'old code meets a newer row' scenario the brief calls out. All pre-existing 205 tests plus these 14 new ones (219 total) pass; uv run mypy src scripts, ruff check, ruff format --check, and lint-imports (4 contracts kept, 0 broken, unchanged from baseline) are all clean; coverage is 88.30%, above the 80% floor. Write paths were not touched -- every store still serializes via model_dump_json() at the model's own current schema_version; only the 15 read call sites changed.

feature_name: Typed OPENALPHA_* config object and in-process .env loading
feature_description: Add a single typed OPENALPHA_* config object (OpenAlphaConfig, pydantic-settings) replacing 9 scattered os.getenv/os.environ call sites in api/app.py and cli.py, plus in-process .env loading for the openalpha CLI (load_dotenv(), invoked once by cli.py#main, never by module import or SDK construction). Real environment variables always win over the same key in .env, which wins over compiled-in defaults. Fixes: the import-time crash from an unguarded int(os.getenv('OPENALPHA_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES')) (now a named ConfigError, never a bare traceback); OPENALPHA_WEB_DIR being read but undeclared in .env.example (now declared); OPENALPHA_HOST/OPENALPHA_PORT being dead variables for 'openalpha serve' (now real precedence: --host/--port > env/.env > default); Dockerfile's CMD hardcoding --host/--port and silently shadowing its own ENV declarations (CMD now reads them via shell-form ${VAR:-default}); and the P0.A Important finding that the README's Python-source setup told users to copy .env.example to .env before running doctor/serve, while .env was never actually read outside Docker Compose. OPENALPHA_LOG_LEVEL stays declared in .env.example, explicitly marked reserved for structured logging (V2-P0B-007), not wired to an unused config field.
acceptance_test: tests/unit/test_cli.py::test_main_entrypoint_loads_dotenv_before_dispatching_to_doctor
notes: pydantic-settings is the one new runtime dependency (7 -> 8), justified and recorded in docs/architecture/ADR-0004-config-and-dotenv-loading.md. Amendment (2026-08-07, same ADR): a follow-up review found the original hand-written .env parser (config.py#_parse_dotenv_text) had two real bugs -- KEY=value # comment silently kept the trailing comment as part of the value (silent credential corruption), and export-prefixed lines were silently dropped rather than handled. python-dotenv was already a mandatory transitive dependency of pydantic-settings (confirmed in uv.lock); load_dotenv() now delegates parsing to its dotenv_values(path, interpolate=False) directly (interpolation explicitly disabled to keep this project's original no-interpolation behavior -- a credential containing a literal ${...} must survive verbatim), and python-dotenv is now declared as an explicit direct runtime dependency (python-dotenv>=1.1,<2) rather than left as an unstated transitive consequence -- runtime dependency count moves 8 -> 9, a second deliberate, recorded exception. Its default logging warning for an unparseable line (via the dotenv.main logger, independent of the verbose argument) is routed to a NullHandler with propagation disabled so a malformed .env line still degrades silently, never a crash, and never new unannounced stderr output. New regression tests cover every awkward-input case: quoted values, a hash inside quotes, an embedded = in the value, CRLF line endings, an export prefix, duplicate keys (last wins), and the no-interpolation guarantee. Separately, tests/unit/test_config.py's autouse _isolated_environ fixture previously cleared only the five OPENALPHA_* variable names, hardcoded in the test file -- it did not clear credential variables, so a shell that had exported e.g. TUSHARE_TOKEN (exactly what this repository's own root .env header comment recommends via `set -a; source .env; set +a`) leaked into every test in the file and broke three real-env-wins precedence assertions reproducibly. The fixture now derives its full clear-list directly from .env.example's declared variable names instead of a second, hand-maintained list that can drift; proven stable by re-running the full suite with seven credential variables exported as bogus values (251 passed, unchanged). Test isolation from a developer's real root .env remains structural, not best-effort, and the CLI-only load_dotenv() call boundary, discover_dotenv()'s cwd-based resolution, and the --host/--port > env/.env > default precedence are all unchanged and re-verified after this amendment -- see the P0.B task report for exact commands and output.
